t.hingol national park@25.5,65.5:
The Hingol River reaches the Arabian Sea through one of the strangest landscapes in Pakistan, and the national park around it is the largest in the country. It covers a huge expanse of dry mountains, dunes and badlands where wind and water have carved the sandstone into towers, buttresses and needles. Two of them have nicknames that every visitor picks up: one the Princess of Hope, a profile against the sky, and the other the Sphinx. The colours range through cream, rust and pale yellow, and the light in the early morning is superb.

The Makran Coastal Highway, opened in the early 2000s, is what makes it reachable. It runs west from Karachi along the Balochistan coast to Ormara, Pasni and Gwadar, a single ribbon of tarmac with sea on one side and desert on the other. Riding it is a matter of distance and heat: long, empty straights, a handful of gentle climbs, and only the odd small village for company. The Buzi Pass section, with its climbs and bends, is where the road does anything interesting, and the views are huge.

Hingol also has something rarer: a pilgrimage. The Hinglaj Mata temple, a cave shrine near the river, is one of the holiest Hindu sites in Pakistan, and every spring pilgrims travel from across the country and beyond to visit it. The place is sacred to Muslims and Hindus alike in local tradition, and the pilgrimage has been going on for centuries. Mud volcanoes in the area, small cones that bubble cold clay, are another local curiosity and also considered sacred.

For the traveller the logistics matter more than the poetry. Mobile coverage is patchy. This is remote country, and the security situation in Balochistan can change; check current advice, ride in daylight, and tell someone your plan. Temperatures in summer are extreme, so the winter months from November to February are the sensible season.

Wildlife is part of the scene, too, with ibex and urial in the hills, and the Hingol river itself holds crocodiles. A quiet visitor at dawn has the best chance of seeing something move.
t.kund malir@25.4,65.5:
Kund Malir is where Pakistan's coastal desert gives you a proper beach. A long crescent of pale sand opens onto the Arabian Sea, with water that goes from pale turquoise at the edge to deep blue beyond, set against a backdrop of bare, folded hills. It is the sort of beach that photographs well and feels slightly unreal, because it is so far from anywhere and so empty. Karachi families do drive out for the day, and on a winter weekend you will find a few tents and food vendors, but on a weekday the sand is yours.

The coast highway passes close by, running between the Hingol hills and the sea, and the road in is some of the best of the whole Makran ride. Near Buzi Pass the tarmac climbs through low mountains and bends in gentle curves, with the sea flashing on one side. It is smooth, wide and almost empty, so a rider can cover distance quickly, though sand drifts across the surface in places and the occasional truck or stray goat deserves attention. Head winds off the sea are common in the afternoon, and the heat, from April to September, is punishing.

The water is clean and often calm, but this is not a resort. There are no lifeguards, the shoreline can drop away steeply, and currents can be strong, so swim close to the shore and never alone. Shade comes from the tents and the odd rock overhang, so bring a hat. A few roadside stalls sell tea and simple food, though what is on offer varies with the season and the day. Carry your own water.

The nearest pumps are in the larger towns along the highway, with Ormara to the west and the towns near Karachi to the east, so fill up beforehand. Overnight camping is possible but should be arranged carefully, and conditions in Balochistan call for sensible planning.

The coastline here has a long history. Ships of Alexander the Great's fleet sailed past on the return from India, according to the ancient accounts, and fishing villages have worked these waters for centuries. Dolphins are sometimes seen from the shore, and the beaches further west host nesting sea turtles, so leave nothing on the sand.
